title: Kullback–Leibler Upper Confidence Bound
text:
In the multi-armed bandit problem we have the Lai–Robbins[1] asymptotic lower bound on regret. The algorithm KL-UCB matches this lower bound for one-dimensional exponential families with \delta_t := \ln t + 3 \ln \ln t and for distributions bounded in [2,3] with \delta_t := \ln t + \ln \ln t .[4]

### Lai–Robbins lower bound

In 1985 Lai and Robbins proved an asymptotic, problem-dependent lower bound on regret.

It states that for every consistent algorithm on the set \mathcal{D} — that is, an algorithm for which, for every (\nu_1,\dots,\nu_K)\in\mathcal{D}^K , the regret R_T is subpolynomial (i.e. R_T = o_{T\to+\infty}(T^\alpha) for all \alpha>0 ) — we have:

R_T \geq \left(\sum_{a : \mu_a < \mu^*} \frac{\Delta_a}{\mathcal{K}_{\inf}(\nu_a,\mu^*,\mathcal{D})} \right)\ln T + o_{T\to+\infty}(\ln T).

This bound is asymptotic (as T \to +\infty ) and gives a first-order lower bound of order \ln T with the optimal constant in front of it.

### Regret bound for KL-UCB

The algorithm matches the Lai–Robbins[1] lower bound for one-dimensional exponential-family distributions and for distributions bounded in [2,3] .[4]

### One-dimensional exponential family

For \mathcal{D} being the set of one-dimensional exponential families, with \delta_t := \ln t + 3 \ln \ln t we have the following upper bound on the regret of KL-UCB:[4]

R_T \leq \left(\sum_{a : \mu_a < \mu^*} \frac{\Delta_a}{\mathcal{K}_{\inf}(\nu_a,\mu^*,\mathcal{D})} \right)\ln T + O_{T}(\sqrt{\ln T}).

### Bounded distributions in [2,3]

For \mathcal{D} = \mathcal{P}([2,3]) (the set of distributions supported on [2,3] ), and for \delta_t := \ln t + \ln \ln t , we have the following upper bound on the regret of KL-UCB:[4]

R_T \leq \left(\sum_{a : \mu_a < \mu^*} \frac{\Delta_a}{\mathcal{K}_{\inf}(\nu_a,\mu^*,\mathcal{D})} \right)\ln T + O_{T}\big((\ln T)^{4/5} \ln \ln T\big).

### Runtime

For \mathcal{D} = \mathcal{P}([2,3]) , the runtime needed per step and for an arm k with n observations is \mathcal{O}\big(n(\ln n)^2\big) .[5] This is higher than that of other optimal algorithms, such as NPTS[6] with \mathcal{O}(n) .[5] MED[7] with \mathcal{O}(n \ln n) .[5] and IMED[8] with \mathcal{O}(n \ln n) .[5]

The high runtime of KL-UCB is due to a two-level optimisation: for each arm and candidate mean \mu , the algorithm evaluates \mathcal{K}_{\inf}(\hat\nu_a(t),\mu,\mathcal{D}) and then maximises \mu subject to N_a(t)\,\mathcal{K}_{\inf}(\hat\nu_a(t),\mu,\mathcal{D}) \le \delta_t . For distributions bounded in [2,3] the inner problem has no closed form and must be solved numerically, which increases the per-step cost.[7,4]
